content:
Publication date: Available online 13 October 2026

Source: Journal of Theoretical Biology

Author(s): Ganesan Alagarasan, Rajeev K. Varshney, Eswarayya Ramireddy

title: Global Anthropogenic Methane Emissions: Bottom‐Up Simulations of Current Trends and Scope for Future Mitigation
content:
Abstract
A technology‐resolved bottom‐up model is used to quantify the current state of global anthropogenic methane emissions and the scope for limiting them in a 2030 to 2050 timeframe. Findings show that with current legislation and “middle‐of‐the‐road” developments in global energy and agricultural systems, anthropogenic methane emissions continue on an upward trend in the next decades. With full implementation of current national plans for methane mitigation, emissions will decline between 2020 and 2030, but not enough to meet the Global Methane Pledge target of a joint global reduction by 30%. The pledge target can be met through full implementation of existing technology, with 70% of mitigation potential in the energy sector. Maintaining low methane emissions beyond 2030 also requires investments into improved waste and wastewater systems and measures to control emissions from livestock and rice cultivation, combined with demand‐side measures to phase‐down fossil fuels and shifts to more sustainable consumption patterns.

title: Dissolved Total Mercury and Methylmercury Fluxes to the Coastal Ocean via Non‐Hydrothermal Submarine Groundwater Discharge
content:
Abstract
Coastal ecosystems are hotspots for biogeochemical cycling of mercury (Hg) and human exposure to neurotoxic methylmercury (MMHg). However, coastal aquifer Hg biogeochemistry remains understudied at a global scale, and the contribution of submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) to global coastal Hg budgets has long been overlooked. In this study, based on a compilation of 44 new observations in the coastline of China and 20 existing observations from around the world, we investigate the distribution and transformation of Hg within global coastal aquifers and estimate non‐hydrothermal SGD‐derived dissolved total Hg (DTHg) and MMHg (DMMHg) flux to the global coastal ocean. We find that almost all coastal aquifers are identified as non‐conservative for both DTHg and DMMHg, and the productive behavior is the most prevalent. We estimate that non‐hydrothermal SGD‐derived DTHg (Monte Carlo mean = 901.8; median = 339.0; interquartile range = 46.6–1005.3 Mg yr−1) rivals riverine discharge, and is ∼3 times and 14 times greater than atmospheric deposition and porewater diffusion from coastal sediments to the global coastal ocean. Notably, non‐hydrothermal SGD is identified as the known largest external source of DMMHg (mean = 77.3; median = 43.4; interquartile range = 14.4–97.7 Mg yr−1) to the global coastal ocean. Hydrothermal SGD systems with elevated Hg concentrations constitute important sources of Hg to specific coastal environments, but their contribution to the global coastal Hg budgets represents a critical knowledge gap. We highlight that SGD‐derived Hg discharge exerts broader and a more direct toxicological pressure on global coastal ecosystems under global change.

title: Coleopteran-active cry gene profiling and insecticidal activity of indigenous Bacillus thuringiensis strains against Holotrichia serrata
content:
Abstract
White grub (Holotrichia serrata F.) is a destructive soil-dwelling pest causing severe yield losses in several agricultural and horticultural crops. Owing to its subterranean habit, chemical control is often ineffective, necessitating sustainable biological alternatives. This study investigated the distribution of coleopteran-active cry genes among indigenous Bacillus thuringiensis strains and evaluated their insecticidal activity against H. serrata. A total of 100 indigenous B. thuringiensis strains isolated from the Western Ghats of India were screened using gene-specific PCR for 12 coleopteran-active cry genes. The most prevalent genes were cry7 (66%), cry26 (65%), cry1b (64%), and cry34 (63%), whereas cry8 and cry9 occurred in fewer than 10% of the isolates. Preliminary bioassays at 380 µg mL⁻¹ identified 20 strains causing > 50% larval mortality. Concentration-dependent bioassays showed that strain NBAIR Bt68 was the most virulent, causing 73% mortality with an LC₅₀ of 149.95 µg mL⁻¹. Highly toxic strains consistently possessed the cry7–cry26–cry34–cry35 gene combination, whereas the total number of cry genes did not correlate with high insecticidal activity. Molecular profiling combined with bioassay evaluation identified indigenous B. thuringiensis strains with promising biocontrol potential and provides insights into the association between cry gene combinations and insecticidal activity against H. serrata.

title: Site, Fertilization and Season Structure the Soil Microbiome and Its Interactions With Bdellovibrio and Like Organisms Predators
content:
The effects of agricultural practices on the soil microbiome, including the microbial predators Bdellovibrio and Like Organisms (BALOs), was performed in agricultural fields at two sites for a year. Communities were qualitatively influenced by season, site and fertilization. A high BALO diversity was found, including novel clades. BALO population dynamics and microbiome‐BALO interactions networks were highly responsive to environmental fluctuations and agricultural practices. This suggests that integrating BALOs in soil microbiome management could benefit agricultural practice.

ABSTRACT
The contribution of predation between bacteria to microbial community dynamics in agricultural soil has hardly been investigated. Here, dynamics of general prokaryotes (GEP) and the predatory Bdellovibrionales (Bd) and Bacteriovoracales (Bac) (Bdellovibrio‐and‐Like Organisms, BALOs) were studied in two agricultural fields differing in organic and mineral inputs for 1 year. Season, but not fertilization, affected absolute sizes of GEP and of BALO communities. 16S rRNA gene analysis identified numerous previously undetected Bd and Bac lineages, with none of the BALOs related to characterized isolates. A few dominant BALO amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) persisted year‐round, whereas others showed seasonal or treatment specific responses. Alpha diversity of the GEP, Bd and Bac communities was influenced by season, with some changes due to fertilization observed for Bd and Bac. Seasonal variation, site and fertilization regime also significantly influenced beta diversity and the structure of BALO–gram‐negative bacterial association networks, revealing distinct community associations under different environmental conditions. Accordingly, we suggest that environmental variation and agricultural practice influence bacterial community structure and are associated with corresponding changes in BALO communities and their potential associations with gram‐negative bacteria. These dynamics may be harnessed to manipulate the soil microbiome to benefit sustainable environmental and agricultural outcomes.

title: Patterns of Functional Redundancy and Anaerobic Metabolic Potential Characterise the Skin Microbiome of a Critically Endangered Sawfish
content:
The largetooth sawfish skin supports a distinct microbiome enriched in anaerobic metabolic and dormancy potential, consistent with microbial persistence under low‐oxygen conditions. Greater among‐individual taxonomic variability coupled with functional redundancy potential supports a lottery‐like mechanism of microbiome assembly. In contrast, the surrounding water column supports greater taxonomic diversity but lower functional redundancy potential, highlighting distinct ecological strategies between host‐associated and free‐living microbial communities.

ABSTRACT
Using shotgun metagenomics of largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) skin and paired pool water samples, we provide the first taxonomic and functional characterisation of a sawfish skin microbiome and assess its ecological distinctiveness, assembly, and resilience relative to the surrounding water column. The skin microbiome was strongly host‐associated and compositionally distinct, with lower taxonomic richness than the water column but dominated by Bacillota, particularly spore‐forming Bacilli. Functional profiling revealed genes associated with sporulation, dormancy, anaerobic metabolism, and peptide transport, consistent with low‐oxygen, low‐flow conditions. In contrast, water‐column microbiomes were more taxonomically diverse and enriched in phototrophic and polysaccharide‐utilisation pathways. Sawfish skin communities exhibited patterns consistent with greater functional redundancy, with gene functions accumulating more rapidly per taxon. Together with greater among‐individual taxonomic dispersion, this pattern is consistent with a host‐filtered, lottery‐like assembly process in which taxonomically variable communities maintain similar functional potential. The enrichment of dormancy and anaerobic pathways suggests the skin microbiome persists through periods of host quiescence and environmental stress while maintaining metabolic potential. Together, these results demonstrate that the sawfish skin supports a resilient, functionally robust microbiome distinct from ambient aquatic communities, highlighting the potential for integrating microbial functional data into conservation strategies for Critically Endangered vertebrates.

title: Source or Sink? Precipitation Shapes Future Terrestrial Carbon Uptake in Australia
content:
Abstract
Nature‐based CO2 removal must deliver sequestration beyond background terrestrial uptake and be resilient to future climate change. Regional‐scale simulations of future terrestrial carbon cycles are needed to establish baselines, map spatial variation in carbon uptake, and guide placement of nature‐based carbon removal projects. Using Australia as a case study, spanning biomes from tropical to semi‐arid, we simulated Australia’s future terrestrial carbon cycle (2015–2100) using a land‐surface model under low (SSP1‐2.6) and high (SSP3‐7.0) emissions scenarios (14 simulations). Simulations indicate that Australia is likely to remain a carbon sink in this century although sink strength is uncertain and strongly linked to variability in precipitation projections. Under SSP3‐7.0, cumulative carbon uptake ranged from 2.0 to 14.2 Pg C with end‐of‐century sequestration rates between 0.01 and 0.22 Pg C yr−1. Under SSP1‐2.6, uptake was lower, ranging from −0.7 to 12.2 Pg C with rates between −0.2 and 0.04 Pg C yr−1. Precipitation was the strongest correlate with carbon uptake, whereas CO2 played a secondary role. Few regions consistently increased uptake across all climate futures, whereas several “hotspots” of decline were identified in southeastern and southwestern Australia. Interannual variability in carbon uptake is projected to increase in the savanna and sparsely vegetated biomes. Our results highlight challenges in identifying regions for nature‐based carbon removal and indicate a weakening terrestrial carbon sink under emissions pathways aligned with Paris agreement goals. This study underscores the value of regional‐scale simulations for informing policies to enhance carbon sinks and the critical importance of precipitation projections to future carbon dynamics.

title: Toward a standard lexicon for ecological forecasting
content: Unprecedented environmental changes challenge our understanding of the natural world, yet critical environmental decisions are made every day. Ecological forecasting provides a mechanism to inform science‐based decision‐making amid accelerating environmental uncertainties by using foundational forecasting principles to anticipate ecological unknowns. However, as an emerging and interdisciplinary field, ecological forecasting lacks unified terminology, limiting cohesion and hindering communication across other forecasting subdisciplines. Here, we examined current use of common forecasting terms by surveying forecasting professionals (n = 109) and synthesizing literature trends (Scopus; 1970–2025) and internet search queries (Google Trends; 2004–2024). Our results informed the development of standardized definitions for “forecast”, “prediction”, and “projection”, and illuminated a disconnect between the goal of aiding decision‐making and the inclusion of decision science in the forecasting process. This work promotes participation and growth in ecological forecasting, helping forecasters meet priority end goals by facilitating communication across forecasting disciplines and within forecasting processes.

title: Slow ecology
How compartmentalization and proliferation shape the splenic T cell repertoire during an immune response to a complex antigen in mice
content:
by Franka Buytenhuijs, Cornelia Tune, Thomas C. Smits, Andrea Schampel, Lisa-Kristin Schierloh, René Pagel, Jürgen Westermann, Johannes Textor

The adaptive immune system recognizes billions of unique antigens using highly variable T cell receptors (TCRs). To what extent TCR features shape the spatial distribution of the TCR repertoire (TCR-R) within lymphoid organs remains unclear. Here, we compared the TCR-R composition in T cell zones (TCZ), B cell zones (BCZ), and germinal centers (GC) of the spleen by analyzing the complementarity-determining region 3 of the beta chain (CDR3β) in microdissected splenic compartments from naïve and immunized mice. While we found substantial differences in TCR-R composition between these compartments, these differences largely disappeared once the effects of compartment size and proliferation were accounted for: During steady state, the few T cells found in BCZs strongly resemble random subsets of those found in TCZs. After immunization, expanded clones started appearing in the TCZ at day 3 and later shifted to the BCZ. GCs harbored even further expanded clones that were grouped into clusters with high sequence similarity. TCR-R differences during the immune response were well explained by a Galton-Watson model of T cell proliferation, suggesting that this could be the central factor shaping the observed TCR-R differences. Similarly, while TCR length and closeness to germline initially showed more pronounced differences between the compartments, our models of random distribution and proliferation explained these differences almost entirely. Hence, our findings suggest that splenic TCR-Rs are shaped predominantly by compartment size and proliferation rates rather than TCR sequence features. This would imply that quantitative assessment of TCR-R dynamics across heterogeneous spatial compartments during an immune response is only possible when these effects are explicitly accounted for.

title: MEGH-DDI: MolT5-driven edge-aware graph learning with Hop2Token representation for drug–drug interaction prediction
content:
by Li Zhou, Yun Zuo, Wenying He, Zhaohong Deng

Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) are critical in pharmacology, as synergistic or antagonistic effects between co-administered drugs can enhance therapeutic outcomes or cause toxicity, posing major challenges for drug safety assessment and new drug development. Current molecular representation methods often fail to capture dynamic substructure relationships or semantic interactions among functional groups. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes MEGH-DDI, a multimodal framework that integrates complementary molecular representation learning with graph-structure dynamic perception. The framework employs a dual-channel semantic module that combines Mol2vec-based substructure representations with MolT5 chemical language embeddings, while SHAP-based dynamic feature selection reduces redundancy. For fine-grained structural modeling, we introduce an edge-aware GCNII equipped with bond-level attention to distinguish different types of chemical bonds. Furthermore, the Hop2Token module converts multi-hop neighborhoods into token sequences, enabling Transformer-based modeling of high-order substructure dependencies. Experimental results demonstrate that MEGH-DDI achieves competitive performance across both transductive and inductive settings. On the DrugBank dataset, MEGH-DDI attains an accuracy of 98.36% in the transductive task, outperforming earlier baselines and surpassing recent state-of-the-art methods, with both AUC and AP exceeding 99.7%. On the ChChMiner dataset, MEGH-DDI achieves an F1 score of 99.05%, improving over the best existing method by 2.74 percentage points. In the inductive settings, MEGH-DDI achieves competitive performance across most evaluation metrics on both datasets, showing advantages over competing methods on several key metrics. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of MEGH-DDI in predicting DDI involving previously unseen drugs and its potential to generalize to complex DDI prediction scenarios. To enhance interpretability, MEGH-DDI incorporates a three-level mechanism spanning atoms, chemical bonds, and topological paths, highlighting key atoms and bond contributions. Overall, MEGH-DDI provides an efficient, accurate, and interpretable solution for drug safety assessment and new drug discovery. Code and datasets are available at https://github.com/Lilyjoys/MEGH-DDI, and a free web platform is provided at http://www.edgh-ddi.com.

title: Cellular diversity in neural organoids is critical for neurodegenerative disease modeling
content:
by Shiying Liu, Shi-Yan Ng

Neuroinflammation and vascular dysfunction are hallmarks of most neurodegenerative diseases. For organoids intended to model neurodegeneration, immune, and vascular cells should therefore be considered fundamental components, rather than optional additions. Neuroinflammation and vascular dysfunction are hallmarks of most neurodegenerative diseases. This Perspective argues that immune and vascular cells need to be fundamental components of organoids intended to model neurodegeneration, rather than optional extras.

title: Deficiency of placental GDF15 causes fetal growth restriction by inhibiting fetal hepatic STAT3-IGF2 axis
content:
by Xiao Peng Liu, Xiao Zhang, Chun Xia Cai, Miao Miao Qin, Xiang Kai Leng, Jia Hao Chen, Yi Fan Han, Jun Ying Xiao, Jia He Huang, Jiang Wei Wu

Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a major cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality, yet its underlying mechanism remains elusive. Here, we show that growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) levels are significantly reduced in the placenta and fetal circulation in mouse and pig FGR models and correlate positively with fetal weight. Placenta-specific GDF15 deficiency causes FGR, while placenta-specific Gdf15 mRNA delivery through targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) effectively alleviates FGR. Mechanistically, placental GDF15 is a major contributor to the fetal circulating GDF15 pool and enters the fetal compartment, where it activates the hepatic STAT3 signaling pathway to stimulate IGF2 production during pregnancy. Placental GDF15 deficiency decreases hepatic STAT3 phosphorylation and IGF2 levels in fetuses. Inhibition of STAT3 in primary mouse fetal hepatocytes blocks GDF15-induced IGF2 upregulation. Placenta-specific Gdf15 mRNA-LNP administration rescues the decreased hepatic p-STAT3 and IGF2 levels in FGR fetuses. Collectively, our findings identify a placenta-fetal liver metabolic axis where placental GDF15 promotes fetal growth by activating the fetal hepatic STAT3-IGF2 pathway, revealing a potential therapeutic target for FGR.

title: A systematic fluorescently tagged protein toolkit for dissecting apical extracellular matrix patterning in C. elegans
content:
by James Matthew Ragle, Murugesan Pooranachithra, Guinevere E. Ashley, Emma Cadena, Batia Blank, Katelyn Kang, Cincy Chen, Aditree R. Bhowmick, Soraya H. Mercado, Tabatha E. Wells, John C. Clancy, Andrew D. Chisholm, Jordan D. Ward

Barrier epithelia are shielded from the external environment by their apical extracellular matrices (aECMs). The molecular complexity of aECMs has challenged understanding of their organization in vivo. To define the molecular architecture of a model aECM we generated a toolkit of 105 fluorescently tagged aECM components using gene editing in C. elegans, focusing on proteins secreted by the epidermis to form the collagen-rich cuticle. We developed efficient pipelines for modular protein tagging and rapid fluorophore swapping. Most tagged collagens were functional and exhibited exquisitely specific patterning across stages, cell types, and matrix substructures. We define multiple reference markers for key substructures including the little-understood cortical layer, as well as the helical crossed fiber arrays that function as a hydrostatic skeleton to maintain organismal shape. We further tagged 30 members of key aECM protein classes including proteases, protease inhibitors, and lipid transporters. Our standardized markers will allow dissection of the mechanistic basis of aECM spatiotemporal patterning in vivo.

title: Oxytocin receptor signaling in the dorsal lateral septum is essential for social transmission of food preference in mice
content:
by Hanyu Fu, Zhiqiu Liu, Jingwei Zhou, Luyao Zhang, Cai Liu, Dewei Tang, Shuangshuang Zhang, Anan Li, Dejuan Wang

Social learning is a fundamental adaptive strategy that critically shapes decision-making and feeding behaviors. Through the social transmission of food preference (STFP), animals acquire information about food safety via social interactions, forming a food-odor memory that overrides innate preferences and guides subsequent food preferences. However, the neural mechanisms through which social cues durably influence feeding preferences remain unclear. Here, we identify the lateral septum (LS) as a key node in STFP. We show that LS neuronal activity increases following social learning and reliably distinguishes between socially cued and uncued foods. Chemogenetic inhibition of the dorsal LS (dLS), but not the ventral LS (vLS), abolishes STFP-driven food preference, revealing subregional specificity within the LS. Furthermore, oxytocin receptor (OXTR) signaling within the dLS is required for STFP in mice, where it enhances neuronal excitability through PLC pathway activation. Together, our results reveal a subregion-specific circuit mechanism through which the dLS integrates social information with feeding motivation, and highlight oxytocinergic modulation as a key mediator of socially guided food preferences.

content:

Chaohui Song explains how a time-lapse mode in wildlife cameras enables sustainable monitoring of forest understory phenology.

Zongzhi Wu explains how multi-omics approaches can help characterize soil microbiome responses to future climate change.

title: Managing cropland edges as multifunctional interfaces for sustainable agriculture
content:
Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43017-026-00844-5

Cropland edges are commonly treated as unproductive remnants or generic conservation strips, yet they constitute dynamic and selectively permeable interfaces between cropped fields and surrounding land. Managing complementary edge portfolios, rather than maximizing edge area or prescribing uniform widths, could reconcile production, biodiversity and climate resilience while limiting cross-boundary risks.

title: The Arctic carbon cycle response to changing root and rhizosphere processes amid greening and permafrost thaw
content:
Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43017-026-00832-9

Arctic warming is rapidly transforming belowground processes and carbon cycling. In this Review, the authors synthesize how root and rhizosphere processes shape carbon balance under permafrost thaw and vegetation change and propose integrative approaches to improve mechanistic understanding and model representation.

title: Correction to: Olsenella scatoligenes-derived skatole promotes smooth muscle cell proliferation and migration to aggravate atherosclerosis
content: This is a correction to: Yawen Zhao, Jiarui Chen, Shanshan Zhu, Yingxi Xu, Jiangyuan Zhu, Jialu Yang, Weibin Zhou, Ying Yang, Maohuan Lin, Qian Chen, Min Xia, Yangxin Chen, Yan Liu, Olsenella scatoligenes-derived skatole promotes smooth muscle cell proliferation and migration to aggravate atherosclerosis, The ISME Journal, Volume 19, Issue 1, January 2025, wraf238, https://doi.org/10.1093/ismejo/wraf238

title: Microbial physiological trait shifts link heavy metal remediation to enhanced soil carbon storage potential
content:
Abstract
Widespread and chronic heavy metal pollution resulting from industrial activities has compromised the sustainability of soil ecosystems. Increasing and stabilizing soil carbon storage is central to soil development, but how remediation reshapes soil carbon cycling processes during the mitigation of heavy-metal contamination remains unclear. Here, we tracked genome-scale microbial metabolism, community turnover, and phenotype-level physiological responses during a 120-day remediation of heavy metal-contaminated soils with several decades of pollution histories and resolved their dynamic interplay with microbial carbon use efficiency (CUE) and CO2 emissions. We found that heavy-metal stress accelerated microbial respiratory carbon loss from soils, with contaminated soils exhibiting significantly higher cumulative CO₂ emissions than both nearby uncontaminated and remediated soils. Metagenomic profiles were enriched in oxidative-stress defense and metal-detoxification functions, consistent with elevated maintenance costs that may contribute to enhanced respiration. In contrast, remediation significantly reduced soil CO₂ emissions while increasing microbial growth rate and CUE, indicating a shift toward greater soil carbon storage potential. Raman-based in situ monitoring further showed that biomolecules associated with microbial growth, including phospholipids, nucleic acids, and proteins, increased progressively throughout the remediation process. Structural equation modelling further revealed that microbial physiological traits, particularly metabolic activity and intracellular biomolecular content, exerted stronger direct effects on CUE than community traits, including community stability and life-history strategy. These results identify microbial physiological traits as a key link between environmental stress and soil carbon cycling. Together, these findings suggest that remediating heavy metal-contaminated soils may represent an underappreciated pathway for enhancing terrestrial carbon sequestration.

title: Deoxycholate induces proline provision from Escherichia coli to enhance Clostridioides difficile virulence
content:
Abstract
Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is a refractory enteritis. A key indicator of successful treatment and microbial restoration is the elevation of intestinal deoxycholate (DCA) levels. Nevertheless, a small proportion of patients experience disease recurrence despite this apparent metabolic recovery, the underlying mechanisms of which remain poorly understood. We investigated the ecological dynamics of Clostridioides difficile (CD) and Escherichia coli (EC) under DCA exposure, revealing that DCA exacerbates the severity of co-infection. Specifically, DCA promotes the formation of a robust and dense symbiotic biofilm that confers a substantial survival advantage to CD. Through a combination of in vitro co-culture and validation in a murine infection model, we demonstrated that EC produces substantial quantities of L-proline in response to DCA. This amino acid is converted to D-proline by the proline racemase and subsequently catabolized by the D-proline reductase in CD, thereby enhancing its environmental fitness and pathogenicity within the gut. The indispensable nature of this tripartite interaction was further corroborated using additional EC or CD strains, including isogenic mutants deficient in D-proline reductase, in subsequent murine infection models. These experiments collectively confirm that EC, proline, and the D-proline reductase are all essential components mediating the DCA-induced exacerbation of CDI. In summary, our study elucidates a mechanism by which a DCA environment promotes the exacerbation of CDI through a metabolic cross-feeding interaction between CD and EC. Specifically, EC-derived L-proline serves as a critical nutrient that enhances the fitness and pathogenicity of CD. This finding provides a plausible explanation for the paradoxical phenomenon of CDI recurrence in patients exhibiting elevated intestinal DCA levels.

title: Eco-evolutionary dynamics and environmental detoxification jointly shape bacterial community response to antibiotic perturbation
content:
Abstract
Microbial communities frequently encounter recurrent antibiotic disturbance, yet how ecological, evolutionary, and environmental processes jointly shape community responses remains unresolved. Here, we use priming to describe the history-dependent effect whereby prior exposure alters the response to a subsequent disturbance. Using a 23-species bacterial community exposed to sequential ampicillin pulses, we examined two dimensions of priming. The ecological dimension was manipulated by exposing assembled communities to an antibiotic pre-pulse that could alter species composition before a common high-dose pulse. The evolutionary dimension was manipulated by experimentally evolving individual species for increased ampicillin resistance before community assembly. Community-level pre-pulse exposure shifted composition toward resistant taxa before the main disturbance, reducing subsequent compositional change. Prior resistance evolution had the strongest effect on community dynamics, buffering compositional change during the main pulse, relaxing subsequent selection, and altering community-wide gene expression. This buffering arose from both increased resistance within species and accelerated ampicillin detoxification by a dominant degrader, which transiently reduced antibiotic exposure and promoted the persistence of non-degrading taxa. However, greater resistance did not improve recovery. Because resistance was coupled to competitive dominance, diversity after disturbance remained similar to or lower than in ancestral communities, whereas dominant taxa became further enriched. Together, our results show that antibiotic exposure history reshapes microbial disturbance responses through interacting eco-evolutionary and environmental feedbacks. These feedbacks increase resistance to recurrent disturbance but can constrain recovery, revealing a trade-off between resistance and diversity restoration.

title: Context-dependent siderophore exploitability shapes microbial community structure
content:
Abstract
Siderophores are classically viewed as shared iron-scavenging public goods, yet their ecological roles in multispecies communities remain incompletely understood. Here, we establish a synthetic microbial community to dissect how different siderophores, their uptake compatibility and spatial structure shape iron competition. Using Corynebacterium glutamicum as a model, we show that this siderophore non-producer accesses diverse xenosiderophores, including enterobactin secreted by Escherichia coli. However, exploitation was constrained and co-cultures converged to stable compositions. Dose–response experiments combined with mathematical modelling indicated that the producer retains more effective access to enterobactin than the exploiter. The presence of Pseudomonas putida altered this interaction, as it exploited enterobactin while producing pyoverdine, a siderophore inaccessible to the other community members that restricted their iron access. Across different cultivation scales, community dynamics was strongly influenced by spatial organization and initial composition. These findings identify siderophores as context-dependent iron-allocation agents that can promote microbial coexistence or exclusion.

title: Balancing photosynthesis and respiration in North Pacific protist communities
content:
Abstract
Marine plankton fuel their metabolism through a continuum of trophic strategies, spanning from pure autotrophy to pure heterotrophy, with mixotrophy combining the two modes within a single organism. Different taxa balance these strategies depending on environmental conditions, complicating efforts to link community composition with ecosystem processes. To quantify the transcriptional investment in processes supporting primary production versus respiration along the trophic continuum, we developed the Transcript-informed Productivity (TiP) metric, defined as the ratio of transcripts in photosynthesis-related pathways (e.g. photosynthesis, carbon fixation) to those in both photosynthesis and respiration-related pathways (e.g. respiration, macromolecule degradation). Higher TiP indicates greater transcriptional investment in primary productivity, whereas lower TiP reflects reduced investment in primary productivity and/or increased investment in catabolic activities. We applied TiP across eukaryotic plankton size classes (~1–100 μm) and taxonomic groups using metatranscriptomes collected during three latitudinal expeditions across the North Pacific. By combining TiP with 18S rRNA gene sequence data and cell size characterization via flow cytometry, we show that biomass in more nutrient-rich areas was dominated by larger phototrophic eukaryotic plankton (diatoms) with higher TiP, consistent with elevated net community productivity (NCP). In nutrient-limited areas, eukaryotic pico- and nano-phytoplankton were dominated by Haptophyta and Dinophyta and displayed reduced TiP, suggesting greater reliance on energy from respiration rather than photosynthesis, consistent with mixotrophic strategies supporting these taxa under nutrient limitation. The TiP metric provided taxon-resolved indicators of eukaryotic productivity and respiration and can complement bulk NCP measurements by identifying the taxa contributing most to ecosystem metabolic balance.

title: Bacterial motility in rhizosphere colonization: mechanisms, constraints, and implications for microbial inoculants
content:
Abstract
Although the potential of microbial inoculants for sustainable agriculture and environmental restoration has been widely recognized, their field performance remains highly variable and often unpredictable. Current research and development frameworks for microbial inoculants primarily focus on their plant growth–promoting functions and metabolic traits, often overlooking the ecological processes that determine whether introduced strains can successfully disperse, access, and establish within the rhizosphere. Increasing evidence suggests that successful dispersal and establishment cannot be assumed in the highly heterogeneous conditions of soil systems. Here, we summarize the key mechanisms underlying bacterial motility and discuss its role within the broader framework of microbial dispersal, highlighting how motility-mediated processes contribute to rhizosphere colonization. We propose that bacterial motility represents a key mechanistic determinant of biofertilizer efficacy. Its role extends beyond the ability of inoculant strains to physically reach the rhizosphere, encompassing competitive colonization on the root surface, long-term persistence, and the ability to respond to dynamic root-derived chemical gradients associated with newly developing root tissues. We argue that inoculant motility should be elevated from a passive descriptive trait to a core design parameter that can be systematically incorporated and regulated during the development and optimization of microbial inoculants. We outline a multi-tiered strategic framework for next-generation biofertilizer engineering that integrates strain selection, community design, motility regulation, and deployment strategies, thereby unlocking the full potential of synthetic microbial consortia for sustainable agriculture, ecosystem restoration, and climate change mitigation.

title: Competition between resident rhizosphere bacteria enhances phytopathogen suppression via emergent antagonism
content:
Abstract
Resident bacterial interactions can shape the invasion resistance of rhizosphere microbiomes, but whether interactions between weakly antagonistic resident bacteria can generate emergent antagonism against invading pathogens remains poorly understood. Here, we used a systematic pairwise interaction screening to identify Ralstonia pickettii RAL5 and Acinetobacter oleivorans ACI4 bacterial pair, that together provided a strong suppression of the phytopathogenic Ralstonia solanacearum Rs1115 strain. Although RAL5 and ACI4 monocultures only weakly inhibited pathogen growth, the RAL5–ACI4 co-cultures strongly suppressed the Rs1115, which was associated with asymmetric competition where the RAL5 dominated the ACI4 species. In line with this competitive asymmetry, broad transcriptional reprogramming was detected in RAL5 and only limited stress- and catabolism-associated responses in ACI4. The increased suppressiveness of co-cultures was associated with clear shifts in the extracellular metabolite profile, including the accumulation of candidate antimicrobial metabolites (e.g. a novobiocin-like feature and 4-aminophenol), and with the release of intracellular contents from ACI4 following RAL5-mediated lysis. The observed emergent antagonism also held in greenhouse experiments with tomato, where the RAL5–ACI4 consortium reduced R. solanacearum abundance and bacterial wilt severity relatively much more compared to when either strain was applied alone. Together, these results suggest that competitive interactions between resident bacteria can activate latent biocontrol potential in rhizosphere microbiomes, providing a new approach to harness resident bacterial interactions for enhanced pathogen suppression and biocontrol.

title: Fungi associated with Norway spruce and its bark beetles detoxify spruce defense compounds by conjugation to α-ribose
content:
Abstract
Fungi readily colonize the inner bark (phloem) of spruce and other conifers despite these tissues having a high concentration of antifungal defense metabolites. These compounds include stilbenes, flavonoids, and other phenolic substances, mostly present as glucosides. Yet, the underlying biochemical mechanisms by which fungi resist conifer phenolics remain largely unresolved. Using untargeted metabolomics, structural elucidation and biological and biochemical assays, we investigated how and why fungi metabolize the major phenolics of Norway spruce (Picea abies). Various fungi, including those associated with bark beetles, were found to hydrolyze stilbene glucosides to their corresponding aglucones. Two basidiomycetes, the saprotroph Coprinellus radians and Cylindrobasidium ipidophilum, a symbiont of the Eurasian spruce bark beetle Ips typographus, then converted the stilbene aglucones into α-ribofuranosylated derivatives, revealing a previously unrecognized pathway in tree-colonizing fungi. Ribosylation markedly reduced the antifungal activity of the aglucones and stabilized them against hydrolysis by fungal and I. typographus enzymes, preventing regeneration of the toxic aglucones. Ribosylation was also correlated with increased growth on spruce bark-containing medium. Hence, the ability to overcome major conifer bark defenses by conversion of toxic stilbene aglucones to non-toxic α-ribosides may explain the successful colonization of this tissue by fungi, some of which support I. typographus attack.

title: Free ammonia stress rewires microbial signaling networks and constrains metabolic cooperation in oxygenic photogranules
content:
Abstract
Free ammonia (FA) is a prevalent chemical inhibitor in wastewater ecosystems, yet its ecological impacts on microbial communication and cooperation remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrated that FA stress restructured the community function of oxygenic photogranules (OPGs) by rewiring signaling-associated regulatory networks and redirecting cellular energy allocation. Temporal profiling of extracellular signaling molecules and intracellular regulatory molecules, integrated with metagenomic and metatranscriptomic analyses, revealed a concentration-dependent reconfiguration of microbial signaling. Under low FA exposure (≤1.0 mg/l), diffusible signal factor- and indole-3-acetic acid -associated pathways were more active, coinciding with photogranules consolidation and efficient nitrogen removal. At moderate FA stress (5.0 mg/l), the regulatory landscape shifted toward acyl-homoserine lactone-associated signaling and bis-(3′-5′)-cyclic dimeric guanosine monophosphate-mediated intracellular regulation, consistent with enhanced aggregation and stress adaptation. In contrast, severe FA stress (25.0 mg/l) broadly attenuated signaling-associated pathways, weakened metabolite cross-feeding networks, impaired energy generation, and increased maintenance-related energetic demands. Under these constraints, microbial populations appeared to shift from cooperative metabolism toward self-maintenance-oriented carbon metabolism, evidenced by activation of the carbon-efficient glyoxylate shunt. Collectively, these findings suggest that FA-induced signaling disruption constrains microbial cooperation through cellular energy limitation, highlighting energy allocation as a key determinant of microbial social stability in phototrophic wastewater microbiomes.

title: Differential aggregation properties among Baltic Sea picocyanobacterial strains impact their export
content:
Abstract
Picocyanobacteria contribute significantly to carbon export but the mechanism by which their biomass is transported to depth is unclear. By analyzing 16S rRNA gene sequences from sediment trap material and size-fractionated water samples from different depths in the Baltic Sea, we show that picocyanobacterial contribution to phytoplankton biomass export was largely proportional (70%–90%) to their surface water abundances. However, we also found that both cell aggregation (enrichment in >10 μm fraction) and sedimentation (trap enrichment) varied among Synechococcus ASVs (amplicon sequence variants). A robust linear relationship was identified between ASV enrichment in traps and ASV enrichment in the >10 μm fraction, suggesting that cell aggregation is a direct determinant of Synechococcus sedimentation. Seasonal abundance patterns were similar among the dominant aggregate-forming ASVs but distinct from those of single-cell ASVs, suggesting aggregate/colony formation being an important trait in determining distribution of Synechococcus strains and their response to environmental conditions. Correlating microscopy- and sequence-based abundances further allowed us to propose genotypes for the dominant Baltic Sea colonial picocyanobacterial morphotypes. Our results provide in situ data linking phenotypic characteristics of picocyanobacteria with sedimentation properties and several lines of evidence for a quantitative dependency between surface water picocyanobacterial aggregate/colony formation and sinking. These findings are important for our understanding of mechanisms involved in export of pico-sized phytoplankton biomass from the photic zone to depth and emphasize the need to investigate occurrence and environmental regulation of cell aggregation in other picophytoplankton-dominated waters (e.g. open ocean gyres).

title: Oxygen-dependent metabolism of dissolved organic matter in hypoxic marine environments
content:
Abstract
Low-oxygen marine environments are dynamic hotspots where microbial activity and dissolved organic matter (DOM) cycling are altered, with implications for understanding ecosystem responses to intensifying anthropogenic pressures. The hypoxic barrier hypothesis (HBH) proposed a mechanism by which DOM cycling could be altered under hypoxia by the inhibition of non-respiratory oxidase enzymes, whereas respiration continued. To investigate oxygen-dependent changes in DOM composition and consequences of the HBH, we combined controlled mesocosm experiments with non-targeted metabolomics to identify classes of compounds that accumulate in hypoxic treatments. Many of these compounds require non-respiratory oxidase enzymes for catabolism in Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) metabolic maps, and when tested in experiments with microbial communities, their catabolism was inhibited by hypoxia, validating the concept of oxygen-dependent DOM (ODDOM). The identified ODDOM molecules displayed chemical characteristics associated with increased DOM stability, including increased aromaticity, carbon oxidation state, and decreased saturation. In a meta-analysis of Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS) datasets from three oceanographic cruises that included samples collected across oxygen gradients and within oxygen minimum zone (OMZ) waters, molecules with chemical properties similar to the mesocosm-derived ODDOM accumulated within the oxycline of the North Pacific Ocean. In the mesocosm experiments, the growth of many microbial taxa was unaffected by hypoxia, and others were either stimulated or inhibited by hypoxia, suggesting unexplored complexity in microbial adaptations to oxygen concentrations in this range. These findings suggest that hypoxia can mechanistically constrain enzymatic pathways determining DOM bioavailability, with implications for microbial carbon cycling and microbial evolution in expanding ocean OMZs.

title: Lives in a gram of soil: linking life cycle biology to soil ecology
content:
Abstract
Soils are among the most diverse but least understood environments on the planet. Just below our feet, secluded from our sight, we find complex communities of bacteria, fungi, protists, and animals. These communities organize themselves in both time and space, from fast to slow growers, from decomposers to predators, from early colonizers to late arrivers. Despite a growing understanding of community dynamics, the lives of organisms within the soil often remain poorly understood: how do organisms grow, propagate, and disperse within their particle-packed environments? In this essay, I reflect on the microbial life cycles found in soils. Starting from a single gram of soil collected on our campus, I explore the conceptual building blocks underlying life cycle biology, how life cycles emerge within their environment, and how they are coupled between species. Microbes express widely diverse life cycle motifs with many unique life stages promoting growth and/or propagation. These life stages have a major impact on community ecology; they determine the fate of microbes within soils and affect how, when, and where microbes interact. A life cycle perspective is thus essential for deepening our understanding of the community dynamics that unfold underfoot.

title: Natural transformation drives large-scale genome mosaicism in human gut bifidobacteria
content:
Abstract
Although horizontal gene transfer drives bacterial diversification, its contribution to chromosome-scale variation in human gut commensals remains unclear. This study demonstrated that human-associated bifidobacteria undergo extensive chromosomal transfer through natural transformation. Comparative genomics of coexisting Bifidobacterium pseudocatenulatum isolates from a single individual revealed extensive recombination signatures between the lineages. We experimentally reproduced this recombination by co-culturing strains, resulting in the transfer of multiple chromosomal regions and generation of mosaic genomes. Individual recombination tracts reached up to 247 kb per site, with cumulative replacements accounting for up to 28.9% of the recipient chromosome. These transfers occurred with heat-killed donors or purified DNA and were abolished by DNase, thereby identifying natural transformation as the underlying mechanism. Furthermore, we observed that environmental factors strongly influenced transformation frequency, suggesting that gut environmental conditions play a role regulating this process. Using natural transformation, we established a simple markerless genome-editing method that enables efficient gene deletions. Deletions of the Tad pili, ComEA–ComEC, or DprA–ComM–YraN gene clusters abolished transformation, defining the core machinery. The conservation of these genes across the genus Bifidobacterium and experimental demonstration of natural transformation in B. longum and B. breve indicate that natural transformation capacity is widespread within the genus. Our findings establish natural transformation as a key mechanism that promotes genome plasticity and contributes to adaptive evolution in bifidobacteria, thereby expanding our current understanding of horizontal gene transfer in the human gut microbiota.

title: Isolation of Allocrenothrix methanica reveals distinct ecophysiologies of filamentous methanotrophs and adaptations to O2 limitation
content:
Abstract
Ferdinand Cohn observed abundant filamentous bacteria in drinking water wells in 1870 that he named Crenothrix polyspora. Subsequent research has revealed the methanotrophic metabolism of Crenothrix bacteria and their disproportionately high activity in stratified lakes compared to unicellular methanotrophs, yet laboratory cultivation has proven elusive, leaving the ecophysiology of Crenothrix bacteria largely unknown. Here we report the isolation of two methanotrophic strains of the “lacustrine Crenothrix” clade from an iron-rich wetland and reveal their unique cell biology and ecology. We demonstrate that the strains are microaerobic and grow as filaments of cells, which are connected by unidirectionally oriented structures. The strains have broad genomic repertoires for addressing O2 limitation that are uniquely associated with lacustrine Crenothrix compared to related clades based on genome data. Aligning with laboratory observations, we identify lacustrine Crenothrix bacteria along potential redox gradients in the wetland at iron-rich snow sites, and we also detect such bacteria in diverse global ecosystems based on public metagenome searches. Together, our data strongly point to an ecophysiology of lacustrine Crenothrix bacteria that is tightly linked to O2 limitation, and we propose that the strains uniquely store or share metabolic intermediates between cells in filaments to thrive under such conditions. Our cultivation-based findings for these strains, which we name Allocrenothrix methanica, provide new insights into the diversity, evolution, and ecology of filamentous methanotrophs, connecting over 150 years of microbiology research and opening vast new opportunities to investigate bacteria contributing to the global methane cycle under O2 limitation.

title: Seawall‐Induced Isolation Alters Hydrological‐Biogeochemical Conditions in Coastal Wetlands
content:
Abstract
Coastal wetlands are increasingly impacted by tropical cyclones and storm surges. Seawalls and levees built to reduce these hazards disconnect wetlands from adjacent uplands, yet their hydroecological effects remain poorly understood. Using continuous hydrological observations in Chongming Island, Changjiang Estuary, China, we compared seaward and landward wetlands separated by a seawall. CTD sensor data, water quality measurements, and plot surveys revealed that seawall construction weakens tidal connectivity and reduces hydrological exchange landward. Seaward wetlands exhibit tidal‐dominated dynamics with higher salinity and lower chlorophyll (CHL), chemical oxygen demand (COD), and total organic carbon (TOC), associated with presence of Phragmites australis. Interior wetlands show reduced salinity, higher values of CHL, COD and TOC, stronger rainfall‐driven responses, and are characterized by more terrestrial vegetation species. These findings suggest that seawalls can substantially alter wetland hydrodynamics and ecosystem structure, highlighting the importance of incorporating hydrological connectivity into seawall design to sustain wetland functions.

title: Decadal Sea Level Variability Along the U.S. East Coast: Roles of Extratropical Versus Tropical Climate Modes Over the North Atlantic Ocean
content:
Abstract
Coastal decadal sea level anomalies (SLAs) in the U.S. east coast (USEC) play a critical role in modulating coastal flooding frequency, yet relative influences of tropical versus extratropical climate modes over the North Atlantic remain unresolved. By integrating observations, simulations from simplified dynamical models and climate models, we show that remote forcings drive the most USEC decadal SLAs since 1950, with approximately half of this signal transmitted via westward‐propagating Rossby waves. Notably, the tropical climate modes, the Atlantic Meridional Mode (AMM) and Atlantic Nino, exert comparable remote influences as the extratropical climate modes in the USEC. We identify a key mechanism that AMM‐related wind and buoyancy forcings act constructively in the northwest Atlantic, amplifying decadal SLAs in the north USEC. Our findings reveal that tropical Atlantic variability is an important, yet previously underappreciated, driver of regional sea level, underscoring its critical role in decadal predictions and flood risk assessments.

title: Enhancement of the Nighttime Ocean Cool Skin Effect by Natural Surfactants
content:
Abstract
The ocean interface brightness temperature is sensitive to the biologic activity reflected by the chlorophyll‐a concentration (Chla) in the upper layers of the oceans. This is shown using sea surface skin temperatures Tskin retrieved from spectra recorded by the Infrared Atmospheric Sounder Interferometer and collocated measurements of bulk temperatures Tbulk by drifters and of Chla from a daily Copernicus multi‐satellite product. The results demonstrate that |ΔTobs| $\vert {\Delta }{T}_{\text{obs}}\vert $, with ΔTobs=Tskin−Tbulk<0 ${\Delta }{T}_{\text{obs}}={T}_{\text{skin}}-{T}_{\text{bulk}}\,<  0$, increases with Chla, particularly when the surface wind is weak. This finding is attributed to the hydrodynamic damping of ocean near surface turbulence by biogenic surfactants that leads to an increase of the cool‐skin thickness. Parametric formulations of the cool skin temperature difference and thickness depending on both the wind speed and Chla are proposed. This enables to assess the global potential impact of biogenic surfactants on interfacial temperatures that is mostly a coastal and polar phenomenon.

title: Correcting Unwrapping Errors Toward Reliable Rock Glacier Velocity From InSAR Time Series
content:
Abstract
Rock Glacier Velocity is an Essential Climate Variable Permafrost Quantity, providing a quantifiable indicator of mountain permafrost evolution. Despite its wide usage, multi‐temporal InSAR often substantially underestimates rock glacier velocities compared to ground‐based measurements, limiting its reliability. In this study, we identified ubiquitous unwrapping errors in Sentinel‐1 interferograms as the dominant source of underestimation over 17 rock glaciers in the European Alps. To address this issue, we developed a method combining manual correction for short‐span interferograms and phase‐closure‐based correction for long‐span interferograms. Our method substantially mitigated velocity underestimation for the rock glacier Grosses Gufer, increasing the maximum velocity from ∼0.5 to ∼2.5 m/yr and achieving strong agreement with independent GNSS data (R2=0.79 ${R}^{2}=0.79$, p<0.01 $p<  0.01$) for velocities ≤2.5m/yr ${\le} 2.5\,\text{m/yr}$. This approach provides an important step toward reliable construction of Rock Glacier Velocity time series using InSAR, enhancing its application in alpine permafrost studies.

title: The 2 May 2025 Mw 7.4 Drake Passage Earthquake: Insights Into Tectonics at the Shackleton Fracture Zone–Chilean Trench Transition
content:
Abstract
On 2 May 2025, an Mw 7.4 earthquake occurred ∼120 km off the southern tip of Tierra del Fuego, at the transition of the Shackleton Fracture Zone and the Chile Trench. This event exhibits reverse‐faulting mechanisms with relatively steeply dipping planes and is the largest recorded along this complex plate boundary. Most aftershocks have similar mechanisms, although some show strike‐slip and normal faulting. To better resolve the activated fault system under limited station coverage, we relocated events and incorporated pP‐sP phases identified using a trained classifier to refine focal depths. A multichannel seismic reflection line provides additional insights into the structure of the subduction complex. We infer that the mainshock nucleated on the subduction interface or within the plate of the southernmost Chilean subduction system, with aftershocks marking activation of steeper structures. This behavior emphasizes how convergent and strike‐slip fault systems interact to complicate earthquake rupture at plate boundary transitions.

title: Magnitudes and Rates of Strength‐Drawdown Modulate Injection‐Induced Seismicity
content:
Abstract
Accurately forecasting injection‐induced seismicity remains a major challenge that is critically important for energy production and storage as controlling mechanisms are complex and remain opaque. We clarify key processes by following time‐histories of bespoke parameters anticipated to control strength reduction (drawdown) through overpressure during fluid injection. Injection‐driven radial overpressure fields motivate key parameter groups representing magnitudes (r∂P∂r $r\frac{\partial P}{\partial r}$) and rates (t∂P∂t $t\frac{\partial P}{\partial t}$) of strength‐drawdown. We emphasize these physics‐informed features as inputs embedded in a two‐stage machine learning (ML) architecture applied to high‐resolution microseismic and injection data from the Utah FORGE and EGS Collab stimulation experiments. Permuted models, selectively including then excluding these physically‐inspired terms, predict temporal seismic evolution and capture trends and peaks with testable and discernible fidelity. Improved predictions result from including these diagnostic parameters—confirming that the derived physical parameters mechanistically mediate seismicity. The magnitude of strength drawdown (r∂P∂r $r\frac{\partial P}{\partial r}$) dictates the size and localization of seismic events during phases of steep spatial pressurization—particularly early in the injection phase near the well. Conversely, t∂P∂t $t\frac{\partial P}{\partial t}$ governs the timing and rate of onset of seismic activity during rapid injection transients, accounting for elapsed‐time effects. Our approach demonstrates the broader benefits of embedding physics‐guided features into ML frameworks toward mitigation of seismic hazard.

title: A Hybrid Superdroplet–Bin Microphysics Approach Reveals How Large Salt Particles Trigger Rain in Non‐Precipitating Warm Convective Clouds
content:
Abstract
This study develops a Superdroplet‐Bin hybrid microphysics scheme within the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to investigate hygroscopic seeding of warm convective clouds. The Super‐droplet method describes 3D transport, deliquescence, condensation, and collision‐coalescence growth of seeding agents or solution droplets, while the spectral bin method simulates liquid‐phase processes. Idealized simulations indicate that seeding full‐spectrum salt near cloud base can produce a maximum accumulated precipitation of 11.59 mm in 3 h. Further sensitivity experiments on seeding particle size reveal that rainfall enhancement primarily originates from particles ≥4 μm, with 5 μm yielding the most pronounced effect. This is because particles ≥4 μm can nucleate to form droplets ≥20 μm, shifting collision‐coalescence from the low‐efficiency regime below 20 μm to the high‐efficiency regime between large and drizzle‐sized droplets. The tail and rain‐embryo effects are identified as the dominant mechanisms, competition alone cannot effectively broaden the droplet spectrum or trigger precipitation.

title: An Improved Dust Emission Modeling With Multiple Endmember Spectral Mixture Analysis
content:
Abstract
Traditional dust emission schemes typically rely on photosynthetic vegetation (PV) alone when parameterizing key surface properties. Here, we integrate five endmembers from the multiple endmember spectral mixture analysis (MESMA), namely PV, non‐photosynthetic vegetation, bare soil, dark surface, and ice/snow (IS), into a well‐established dust emission scheme to simultaneously constrain surface roughness and the erodible fraction, avoiding the common reliance on PV alone as in traditional dust emission schemes. By evaluating three severe dust events in East Asia in 2021, 2023, and 2024, the MESMA‐constrained configurations reduce total dust emissions by 22.2%–49.7% and show substantially improved agreement with station observations. By enabling a physically realistic characterization of dryland surface heterogeneity through multiple endmembers, this approach substantially alleviates the systematic overestimation that is typical when using PV‐based parameterizations.

title: Impacts of Sea Surface Temperature Warming Pattern Biases on Tropical Cyclone Activity and Hazard
content:
Abstract
Most climate models simulate greater warming in the equatorial eastern Pacific than in the west under historical forcing, resulting in a reduced zonal sea surface temperature (SST) gradient and a weakened Walker circulation. This contrasts with observed trends and highlights a persistent model–observation discrepancy with far‐reaching impacts on regional climate extremes. The authors' previous work showed that reducing mean‐state biases in a coupled model yields SST trends more consistent with observations. Here, we downscale tropical cyclones (TCs) from these simulations and find that a strengthened zonal SST gradient is associated with increased TC frequency and hazards in the North Atlantic and suppresses activity in the South Pacific. In future projections, both biased and bias‐corrected models simulate relative eastern Pacific warming, yet their TC responses differ regionally, with the bias‐corrected model projecting greater TC activity and hazards over the North Atlantic.

title: A Generalized Analytical Model for Marine Gas Hydrate Stability Zones With Thermodynamically Constrained Pressure–Temperature Phase Boundary
content:
Abstract
Accurate thermodynamic delineation of marine gas hydrate stability zones (GHSZs) is a fundamental prerequisite for assessing methane hydrate inventories, quantifying the vulnerability of methane dissociation to climate change, and evaluating overpressure‐induced submarine geohazards. However, the commonly adopted pressure–temperature phase boundaries are predominantly calibrated under idealized conditions and fail to capture natural marine conditions, leading to persistent uncertainties and systematic biases in global GHSZ delineation. Here, we assemble a globally representative dataset of field‐constrained hydrate records to refine and calibrate a thermodynamically constrained phase boundary tailored to natural marine environments. The resulting field‐calibrated phase boundary features clear physical interpretability, robust extrapolation reliability, and enables the GHSZ boundary depth to be calculated directly using an explicit closed‐from analytical solution. The analytical model delineates thermodynamically admissible GHSZ configurations and is validated against global observations for the prevalent single basal‐interface case, providing an efficient framework for regional‐to‐global hydrate‐related assessments.

title: The ambitions and limitations of climate assemblies
content:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02764-0

Climate citizens’ assemblies are gaining traction worldwide as a way to involve the public in climate governance. Now a study demonstrates that although these assemblies propose more ambitious recommendations than existing climate policy, these recommendations vary across contexts and have limited impact on policy decisions.

title: Strengthening Rio Convention implementation architecture through reciprocal learning
content:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02777-9

As the Rio Conventions mature from negotiating commitments towards delivering them, strengthening implementation has become an urgent priority. We argue for greater cross-convention learning within the context of institutional architecture to accelerate progress on climate, biodiversity and land degradation.

content:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02755-1

Deliberative citizen participation, such as climate assemblies, has been promoted in climate governance. This study finds that, although assemblies proposed more ambitious recommendations than existing climate policy, these recommendations rarely translated into actual policy decisions.

title: Progressive oxidative weathering raised sub-arc mantle fugacity on the Archaean Earth
content:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02119-6

Progressive oxidative weathering in the Archaean may have raised the proportion of oxidized sulfur recycled during subduction, suggesting a feedback between the surface and increasingly oxidized arc magmatism, according to sulfur in apatite inclusions.
