content:
Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 13 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01382-z

In this Review, Dong and colleagues overview recent developments in mosquito-targeted malaria control, highlighting Anopheles population modification (rendering mosquitoes Plasmodium-resistant) and Anopheles population-suppression strategies based on gene drive technology, engineered microorganisms, vaccines and drugs, and discuss key knowledge gaps and the responsible implementation of these approaches in conjunction with existing malaria interventions.

title: Current dynamics, drivers, and vertical thermal structure  around Sir Bu Nair Island (Arabian/Persian Gulf)
content:
Current dynamics, drivers, and vertical thermal structure around Sir Bu Nair Island (Arabian/Persian Gulf)
Geórgenes H. Cavalcante, Filipe Vieira, Rita Bento, Aaron Bartholomew, and John A. Burt
Ocean Sci., 22, 3165–3183, https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3165-2026, 2026
Sir Bu Nair Island hosts some of the healthiest coral reefs remaining in the Arabian Gulf despite extreme summer heat. Using 17 months of observations, we found that tides dominate local currents, while winds and lower-frequency circulation are associated with changes in vertical temperature structure. Regional and local processes interact to create highly variable conditions around the island, with important implications for coral exposure to heat stress.

title: In Vivo Transcriptomics-Based Framework for Systematic Indication Expansion
content: Capturing the systemic effects of drugs in vivo remains a fundamental challenge for drug repurposing strategies. Here, we present an in vivo transcriptomics-based drug repurposing framework that profiles multi-organ RNA-seq from drug-treated rodents to model systemic drug responses and match tissue-specific drug signatures against a compendium of disease signatures for indication expansion. We applied this framework to semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist originally developed for diabetes and subsequently expanded for several other indications. By harmonizing more than 900 human disease transcriptomic signatures via agentic AI and using Z-transformed reversal of gene expression scoring to quantify drug-disease relationships, our approach successfully recovered established semaglutide indications while deprioritizing Alzheimers disease, an indication for which semaglutide was not effective. Top predictions for common diseases were supported by real-world electronic health record data from the Mount Sinai Health System and several predictions for rare indications are proposed for further investigation. This framework provides a scalable strategy for indication expansion across diverse therapeutic agents, especially investigational compounds for which real-world evidence remains sparse.

title: Unifying N- and O-glycopeptide dissociation methods with expedient electron transfer dissociation
content: The glycoproteome is highly heterogeneous, where each glycosite can be modified by potentially hundreds of glycan compositions. This complexity necessitates methods that can provide glycosite-specific characterization in a high-throughput manner. Electron transfer dissociation (ETD) is particularly valuable for glycopeptide analysis, where it is critical for glycosite localization in O-glycopeptides and often produces higher quality spectra than higher energy collisional dissociation (HCD) for N-glycopeptides. Despite this, lower quality HCD spectra are often favored in high-throughput glycoproteomics experiments because the near instantaneous fragmentation of HCD results in faster MS/MS spectral acquisition relative to ETD. In short, overhead times for ETD reactions limit acquisition rates and sensitivity that can outweigh its advantages. Here we implement changes to ion handling, scan parallelization, and ion-ion reaction conditions to increase ETD MS/MS acquisition rates on the Orbitrap Tribrid MS platform. We explore fundamental parameters of ETD ion-ion reactions, including reaction q-values (i.e., Mathieu q-values) and ion-ion reaction time, showing that we can reduce the overhead of ion-ion reaction scan functions and improve the overall synchronization of data acquisition. These optimizations lead to faster spectral acquisition times for ETD MS/MS spectra while maintaining high spectral quality. Ultimately, these improvements allow the ETD scan functions to be nested within ion accumulation times needed per MS/MS spectrum, enabling ETD spectral acquisition to be parallelized within the duty cycle of the instrument and removing the major time cost to doing ETD-based fragmentation. We argue that this expedient implementation of ETD makes ETD-based fragmentation a universally beneficial dissociation method for both N- and O-glycopeptides.

title: Comprehensive calculation of product and ATP yields for glucose fermentation
content: Lignocellulose sugars are degraded anaerobically by microbial communities as part of the carbon cycle, yielding short- and medium-chain fatty acids as intermediates and carbon dioxide and methane as final products. The underlying metabolic network is branched and its product yields depend on environmental conditions. We compiled a pan-catabolic network of the anaerobic digestion of glucose into 11 fermentation products, including alcohols, acids, and ketones. It consists of 75 reactions and incorporates energy conservation via substrate-level phosphorylation and transport-coupled phosphorylation, with ferredoxin, NADH, and quinol as electron carriers. We calculated all net conversions of glucose into fermentation products and their ATP yields. We find 195,629 unique conversions (about 50% with non-zero ATP yield), including known and many novel ones. Conversions with identical product stoichiometry can differ in ATP yield: glucose to propionate and acetate is achieved by different subnetworks with 23 distinct ATP/glucose yields, and even glucose to lactate shows 12 yields ranging from 0 to 4.5. The driving force of the conversions decreases with ATP yield, whereas the number of reactions used does not correlate with it. The known catabolic conversions underlying anaerobic digestion might thus be only the tip of the iceberg.

title: 13C-Metabolic Flux Analysis of Substrate Co-Metabolism in the Methylotrophic Acetogen Eubacterium limosum.
content: Acetogens are promising microbial catalysts for the sustainable production of fuels and chemicals, metabolizing a range of renewable single-carbon (C1) compounds with high energetic efficiency. The major challenge is their energy-limited anaerobic lifestyle, which results in slow growth and a limited product spectrum on individual C1 substrates. We previously showed in the acetogen Eubacterium limosum that co-metabolism of glucose-methanol or CO-methanol mixtures results in substantial improvements in growth and acetate productivity. To investigate the underlying mechanism(s), here we conducted 13C metabolic flux analysis (13C-MFA) of E. limosum grown on a glucose-methanol mixture, as well as in single-substrate controls. The results suggest that the main benefit of glucose cofeeding is not provision of additional ATP, but rather a reduction of flux through the ferredoxin-dependent and kinetically challenging reactions of the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway. Subsequent RNAseq analysis showed no significant differences in the expression level of genes involved in methanol metabolism between cofeeding and methanol-only controls, suggesting this reduction of flux is controlled post-transcriptionally. Most surprisingly, we found that under all growth conditions, flux through pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR) was in the oxidative direction, with cysteine (added as a reducing agent) providing all required gluconeogenic carbon flux under CO2-fixing conditions. This work provides critical insights into the metabolic network of an emerging model acetogen that will facilitate future metabolic engineering efforts to channel flux to value-added products, and highlights the under-appreciated role of cysteine as a carbon source in acetogenic fermentations.

title: PGC-1α Links Estrogen Receptor Signaling to Japanese Encephalitis Virus Replication in Neuronal cell
content: Acute encephalitis due to the viral causative agents, such as Japanese Encephalitis Virus (JEV), remains a leading cause of viral encephalitis in Asia, contributing to high mortality and long-term neurological sequelae. The host factors that modulate JEV replication are not well understood. In this study, we investigated the modulation of JEV infection by estrogen in vitro and in vivo. The results demonstrated that estrogen enhances JEV replication in neuronal cells via estrogen receptor alpha (ER) by modulating peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1 alpha (PGC-1). Since JEV pathogenesis increases cellular production demands, it results in dysregulation of cellular homeostasis, whereas estrogen treatment helps keep cellular health in check. Also, the mouse model exhibited an increased viral burden with protective antibody titers in response to estrogen. Conclusively, this work highlights the mechanistic link of estrogen-driven mechanisms and identifies the ER-PGC-1-axis as a potential target for sex-specific therapeutic interventions.

title: Cardioselective β-blocker Therapy Resolves Staphylococcus aureus Toxin-Induced Innate Immunoparalysis
content: During Staphylococcus aureus sepsis, the pore-forming -toxin (Hla) triggers lytic platelet death and provokes the release of catecholamines that modulate leukocyte effector function. The resulting surge in catecholaminergic action paralyzes host antimicrobial capacity by upregulating interleukin-10 (IL-10), profoundly suppressing the protective interferon (IFN) response to orchestrate innate immunoparalysis. Here, we deconvolute a multi-cellular regulatory pathway in the blood and highlight a pivotal immunological checkpoint, where pharmacological intervention with cardioselective {beta}-blockers uncouples the immunosuppressive cascade, restores host antimicrobial function, and significantly improves survival outcomes.

title: Concentration-dependent inhibition of Streptococcus mutans metabolic activity by purified Croton lechleri latex (sangre de grado) in vitro
content: Background. Chlorhexidine is the reference chemical antiplaque agent, but its adverse effects motivate the search for plant-derived alternatives. The proanthocyanidin-rich latex of Croton lechleri (sangre de grado) is a candidate, yet quantitative concentration-response data against Streptococcus mutans are scarce. Methods. In this exploratory in vitro study, ethanol-purified C. lechleri latex was tested at working concentrations of 3-100% v/v (final in-well concentrations 0.6-20% v/v) against S. mutans ATCC 25175 in a 96-well resazurin assay with dual-wavelength reading (570/600 nm) and correction for medium and latex color. Chlorhexidine 1% (0.2% in-well) was the positive control. Each condition was run in technical triplicate within a single experiment. Data were analyzed by one-way ANOVA, Tukey's test with simultaneous 95% confidence intervals (CI) and four-parameter logistic regression. Results. Metabolic activity decreased monotonically with concentration, from 101.3 +/- 1.7% (vehicle) to 54.0 +/- 4.7% (12%), 15.5 +/- 4.0% (50%) and 8.6 +/- 7.7% (100%), compared with 3.1 +/- 2.8% for chlorhexidine (F(7,16) = 160.7, p < 0.001). The lowest concentration that differed from the vehicle was 6% (difference 17.6 percentage points, 95% CI 2.1-33.1). The estimated half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) was 12.3% v/v (95% CI 9.5-15.1). Differences from chlorhexidine at 50% and 100% were not statistically significant, but their confidence intervals were compatible with differences of up to 28 and 21 percentage points, respectively. Conclusions. Purified C. lechleri latex inhibited the metabolic activity of planktonic S. mutans in a concentration-dependent manner. These preliminary findings do not establish equivalence with chlorhexidine and warrant replication in independent experiments with chemically standardized extracts expressed in mg/mL, determination of MIC/MBC and biofilm models.

title: Quantitative host-response mapping enables phenotypic profiling of viruses detected by virome sequencing
content: Animal-derived viruses have repeatedly caused human outbreaks, motivating efforts to identify and characterize viruses circulating in animals. Virome sequencing has accelerated animal virus discovery, but phenotypic characterization remains difficult to scale. Although generated for viral detection, virome RNA-seq data also capture host transcriptional responses to infection. Here, we developed ViroChart, a comparative transcriptomic framework that quantifies activities across biological pathways and maps diverse mammalian host responses into a common, interpretable low-dimensional space. ViroChart enables clustering of infected samples by host response pattern and quantitative assessment of host response similarity between samples. In virome data sets from wild and farmed animals, some lung samples infected with poorly characterized betacoronaviruses showed host responses resembling those induced by viruses capable of causing fatal disease. ViroChart also revealed host-response heterogeneity in natural infections: among rats with zoonotic rodent-borne viruses, most showed weak responses, consistent with asymptomatic infection, but some showed pronounced inflammation characteristic of acute infection. ViroChart thus enables phenotypic characterization and prioritization of newly detected viruses by leveraging the same RNA-seq data from which their genomes were detected.

title: Genomic and physiological characterization of Neobacillus ammoniipjilus sp. nov. reveals versatile inorganic nitrogen utilization and ammonia-mitigation potential
content: A novel bacterial strain (KR4-4T), was isolated from soil in the Republic of Korea and subjected to polyphasic taxonomic and functional characterization. Phylogenetic analysis based on the 16S rRNA gene sequence placed strain KR4-4T within the genus Neobacillus. Phylogenomic analysis based on 92 bacterial core genes further supported its distinct taxonomic position. Average nucleotide identity and digital DNA-DNA hybridization values between KR4-4T and related Neobacillus type strains were 69.76-82.31% and 18.3-25.9%, respectively, supporting its recognition as a distinct species. Cells were Gram-stain-positive, non-motile, facultatively anaerobic rods, with growth occurring at 15-45 {degrees}C, pH 6.0-8.0, and 0-2.0% (w/v) NaCl. The major cellular fatty acids were iso-C15:0 and anteiso-C15:0, while the major polar lipids included diphosphatidylglycerol, phosphatidylglycerol, and phosphatidylethanolamine. Genome analysis revealed genes associated with inorganic nitrogen transport, nitrate and nitrite reduction, and ammonium assimilation. In liquid culture, KR4-4T removed NH4+-N under aerobic conditions and was able to utilize ammonium, nitrate, and nitrite as individual nitrogen sources, with removal efficiencies of 86.5%, 69.35%, and 62.9%, respectively. The strain also contributed to the reduction of gaseous NH3 in a closed-flask assay. Together, these physiological and genomic characteristics indicate a versatile capacity for inorganic nitrogen utilization and transformation and suggest potential for further evaluation in biological ammonia-mitigation applications. Based on phylogenetic, genomic, phenotypic, and chemotaxonomic evidence, strain KR4-4T represents a novel species of the genus Neobacillus, for which the name Neobacillus ammoniiphilus sp. nov. is proposed. The type strain is KR4-4T (= KACC 24003T = CCTCC AB 2025077T).

title: A silent intergenic locus for efficient and versatile transgene expression in Plasmodium falciparum
content: Genetically modified Plasmodium falciparum parasites expressing transgenes such as fluorescent markers are crucial tools for malaria research. However, current reporter lines often rely on integrated transgene constructs that disrupt the coding sequence of a native gene, potentially affecting progression in the life cycle of the tool parasite line. We identified six candidate Silent Intergenic Loci (SILs): putatively editable intergenic regions without transcriptional activity, where gene insertions occurred in P. falciparum after its divergence from Plasmodium berghei and Plasmodium vivax. We characterised the largest candidate SIL on chromosome 12, SIL12, by integration of a constitutively expressed cytosolic mScarlet reporter. The resulting PfRed12 parasites progressed normally throughout the life cycle, from asexual blood-stage replication to mosquito stages and subsequent liver infection. Importantly, they infected both Anopheles stephensi and Anopheles coluzzii mosquitoes. PfRed12 parasites displayed bright fluorescence in both blood and mosquito stages, making them well suited for live visualisation of parasite transmission. In addition, we used two CRISPR-Cas9 target sites in the mScarlet cassette, one of which we purposely added, to perform efficient re-editing of the transgene. As a proof of concept, we re-edited PfRed12 parasites and integrated an apicoplast metabolic bypass construct, an inducible gametocyte producer construct, and two mNeonGreen reporter constructs. Together, our findings demonstrate that SIL12 permits stable transgene expression without compromising parasite development throughout the life cycle. We established PfRed12 as a new reporter line to study blood- and mosquito-stage development and as a versatile parental line for further genetic engineering.

title: Root exudates enhance the ecological fitness of a non-native PGPR and reshape rhizosphere microbiome assembly
content: Root exudates play critical roles in rhizosphere microbiome assembly. Nevertheless, the molecular mechanisms by which plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) perceive these signals, adapt to the rhizosphere, and influence native microbial communities remain poorly understood. Here, using maize (Zea mays cv. Early Golden Bantam) and the rhizobacterium Priestia aryabhattai AB211, we took a multi-omics approach combining metabolomics, bacterial transcriptomics and proteomics, and rhizosphere metagenomics to elucidate the mechanism underlying this process. Maize root exudates were enriched in diverse carbon and nitrogen metabolites that promoted bacterial growth and induced extensive molecular reprogramming of pathways involved in nutrient acquisition, chemotaxis, motility, stress adaptation, and plant growth promotion, thereby enhancing rhizosphere competence. In field-conditioned soil, AB211 persisted as a core member of the maize rhizosphere microbiome, promoted early seedling growth, and reshaped microbial community composition and function. Root exudates-primed (RE-primed) AB211 further enhanced the enrichment of microbial functions associated with nutrient cycling, quorum sensing, plant growth promotion, and rhizosphere fitness, highlighting the role of root exudates in modulating the rhizosphere-adaptative potential of beneficial bacteria. These findings establish a mechanistic framework linking root exudates composition with PGPR adaptation and microbiome assembly, providing a foundation for engineering ecologically adapted microbial inoculants to improve crop productivity and sustainable agriculture.

title: Bacteriophage susceptibility in clinical Enterococcus faecalis reflects host genomic background and Epa-associated phage adsorption
content: Cytolysin-positive Enterococcus faecalis has been implicated as a disease-associated pathobiont in alcohol-associated hepatitis, motivating development of selective bacteriophage-based strategies. However, strain-level determinants of phage susceptibility remain incompletely understood. We characterized the host range of three E. faecalis phages, {Phi}Ef2.1, {Phi}Ef2.2, and {Phi}Ef2.3Ev, across 45 clinical isolates and investigated bacterial and phage factors associated with adsorption and productive infection. Isolates were characterized by whole-genome sequencing, cytolysin status, antimicrobial resistance determinants, and predicted anti-phage defense systems. Phage susceptibility was measured by efficiency of plating (EoP) and adsorption assays. Thirty-five of the 45 isolates (77.8%), including all 15 cylLs-positive isolates, were susceptible to at least one of the three phages at EoP [≥]0.01. {Phi}Ef2.1 and {Phi}Ef2.2 showed greater activity against cylLs-positive isolates, which also carried higher burdens of predicted antimicrobial resistance determinants and anti-phage defense system types. Analysis of 367 complete E. faecalis RefSeq genomes classified the variable region of the enterococcal polysaccharide antigen (epa) locus into 15 recurrent architecture groups that were associated with phage-specific adsorption patterns. Efficient adsorption did not always result in productive infection, indicating additional post-adsorption barriers. AbiD emerged as a candidate factor associated with reduced {Phi}Ef2.2 productivity, although this signal was prediction-tool dependent, while unexplained post-adsorption blocks suggest the involvement of additional uncharacterized mechanisms. These findings link naturally occurring epa architecture to phage adsorption and highlight distinct post-adsorption constraints on host range, providing a framework for rational phage selection against clinically relevant E. faecalis populations.

title: Staphylococcus aureus enhances influenza A virus replication through modulation of host cell vesicular transport
content: Influenza A virus (IAV) is a major respiratory pathogen that causes substantial morbidity and mortality worldwide. A significant complication of primary IAV infection is secondary bacterial co-infection. Here, we report that Staphylococcus aureus enhances IAV replication through the activity of the surface protein fibronectin-binding protein A (FnbA). The pro-viral activity of FnbA is conserved across multiple IAV strains and is associated with reduced abundance of the host vesicular trafficking proteins VPS26A and VTA1. FnbA does not substantially increase viral protein abundance or alter intracellular distribution. Instead, pro-viral activity is associated with a greater proportion of infectious progeny particles and increased release of infectious virions from infected cells. Thus, we identify FnbA as a bacterial factor that enhances IAV replication and demonstrate that S. aureus can manipulate host cell processes to promote the production and release of infectious virus.

title: Long terminal repeats influence deletion propensity and genome instability in proviruses across major retroviruses
content: A hallmark of retroviral infection is integration of viral genomes into host chromosomes to form proviruses. Most proviruses are defective, particularly in people with HIV receiving antiretroviral therapy, with large internal deletions as a dominant outcome. The contribution of retroviral long terminal repeats (LTRs) in the formation of large internal deletions remains unclear. We used dual-fluorophore reporters based on HIV-1, HIV-2, and HTLV-1 LTRs, integrated at AAVS1 by CRISPR/Cas9, to test whether LTRs influence proviral integrity in the absence of reverse transcriptase or integrase. Cerulean expression was driven by the LTR and mCherry by an independent human promoter. Double-positive (Cerulean/mCherry) cells were a proxy for intact vectors, whereas single mCherry cells indicated latent and/or defective proviruses. Double-positive cells harboured intact vectors for all constructs. Non-inducible single mCherry populations were enriched for extensively deleted proviruses with HIV-1, HIV-2, or HTLV-1 LTRs, whereas the LTR-deficient reporter yielded few single mCherry cells, all with intact proviruses. The presence of LTRs was significantly associated with deleted genomes. HIV-1 and HTLV-1 showed higher observed deletion rates than HIV-2, but this was not statistically significant owing to limited sequence numbers. Single Cerulean populations across all constructs showed recurrent deletions affecting the mCherry cassette and upstream promoter, with short direct repeats at deletion junctions. These likely reflect microhomology-mediated end joining as a contributing repair mechanism during CRISPR/Cas9-mediated integration, in which LTRs may not directly contribute. Together, these data identify retroviral LTRs as contributors to the formation of large internal deletions in proviruses.

title: Tropism of Drosophila innubila Nudivirus in Cell Culture and in Tissues
content: Most viruses are successful because they can infect and exploit specific host tissues for reproduction and transmission. As a result, we often classify viruses by their ability to infect different tissues: respiratory, reproductive and gut, for example. Thus, knowing the tissue and cellular tropism of a virus may elucidate aspects of its biology including routes of transmission and virulence. We studied tropism of the Drosophila innubila Nudivirus (DiNV) in cells and infected hosts. DiNV is a nudivirus, a family of viruses related to the baculoviruses that are relatively large (150-200 nm), contain large double-stranded DNA genomes, and infect different host tissues. Cultured cells stained with an antibody against the DiNV nucleocapsid demonstrated punctate staining in the cytoplasm by confocal microscopy. Electron micrographs of infected cells, on the other hand demonstrated that virions are present in the nucleus. After purification, DiNV was often associated with multimembrane-like vesicles as described for Oryctes rhinoceros nudivirus. We examined tropism in hosts first by sagittal section and found most virus associated with the gut and, to a lesser extent, reproductive tissues. Upon dissection and electron microscopy, we found that DiNV in the gut is primarily in the visceral muscle of the gut and not the lumen as might be expected for a virus if transmitted fecal-orally.

title: Allyl chloride respiration by Dehalobacter shapes the fate of 1,2,3-trichloropropane
content: The synthetic compound 1,2,3-trichloropropane (1,2,3-TCP) is a persistent groundwater contaminant and probable human carcinogen for which effective detoxification pathways remain limited. Under anoxic conditions, microbial transformation of 1,2,3-TCP typically stalls at the intermediate allyl chloride, preventing complete detoxification. Here, we report the enrichment and characterization of Dehalobacter restrictus strain XRTCP, a bacterium capable of coupling dichloroelimination of 1,2,3-TCP with subsequent hydrogenolysis of allyl chloride to propene. While dichloroelimination to allyl chloride has been previously observed, the ability to utilize allyl chloride as a respiratory electron acceptor represents a previously unrecognized metabolic capability. This transformation was linked to microbial growth, with cell densities increasing by up to 74-fold during 1,2,3-TCP reduction and 15.8-fold during allyl chloride transformation. Metagenomic and metaproteomic analyses revealed a diverse repertoire of reductive dehalogenases (RDases), with expression patterns that differed between 1,2,3-TCP and allyl chloride amendments. Notably, a tcpA-like RDase was expressed under both 1,2,3-TCP and allyl chloride conditions, while distinct RDases were preferentially expressed under each substrate, indicating functional specialization within the dechlorination pathway. Despite this metabolic capability, propene formation remained limited due to rapid abiotic transformation of allyl chloride, primarily via reactions with reduced sulfur species, highlighting a critical branching point between biotic and abiotic pathways. These findings demonstrate that allyl chloride can function as a growth-supporting respiratory electron acceptor. More broadly, this work reveals how interactions between microbial metabolism and geochemical processes govern contaminant fate, with implications for improving both monitored natural attenuation and engineered bioremediation strategies for chlorinated solvents.

title: Single-site DNA methylation activates retron defence by enabling effector tetramerisation
content: Retrons are unique among bacterial defence systems in using DNA to sense phage infection. They achieve this by producing multicopy single-stranded DNA (msDNA) that monitors the activity of DNA-targeting phage proteins. Although we understand how extensive msDNA perturbations such as degradation activate retrons, activation by subtle chemical modifications remains enigmatic. Here, we used a structure-function approach to elucidate how single-site msDNA methylation activates Retron-Sen2. The cryo-EM structure of Retron-Sen2 features RcaT, the most prevalent retron effector, sequestered as an inactive dimer within a four-component assembly of previously undescribed architecture. Methylation by DNA adenine methyltransferase disrupts the RcaT-msDNA interaction and exposes a previously occluded interface that enables RcaT dimers to form tetramers, leading to retron disassembly. We show that RcaT dimer-dimer assembly is essential for its toxicity. To assess whether this is a conserved RcaT feature, we characterised additional homologues. RcaTs capable of tetramerisation or higher-order oligomerisation are toxic and form distinct phylogenetic clades from RcaTs that remain dimeric and are non-toxic. Together, our findings provide a paradigm for retron activation by single-site msDNA modifications and showcase how variation in an intrinsic protein property can diversify the toxicity of the same bacterial defence effector during evolution.

title: Pharmacokinetics and Efficacy of the FimH Inhibitor Sibofimloc in Preventing Necrotizing Enterocolitis in Preterm Piglets
content: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a disease in preterm infants associated with an increased abundance of Enterobacteriaceae. FimH, a mannose-binding adhesin on Enterobacteriaceae type 1 fimbriae, mediates mucosal attachment and TLR4-dependent inflammatory cascades. We evaluated the safety, pharmacokinetics, and efficacy of an oral FimH inhibitor (Sibofimloc) to reduce Enterobacteriaceae colonization and prevent NEC in preterm piglets. We performed a 9-d dose-escalation safety study (10, 25, 50 mg/kg BID) assessing absorption and tolerability and a 10-d randomized efficacy study. Piglets in the efficacy study received an infant formula diet with or without oral sibofimloc (40 mg/kg BID), or donor human milk (DHM) as a healthy control. NEC incidence, tissue histopathology, and gut microbiota composition via metagenomic whole-genome sequencing (WGS) were evaluated. Systemic exposure data reveal that sibofimloc was dose-dependently absorbed, while plasma levels decreased from postnatal day 2 to day 8, indicating reduced drug absorption with maturation of the intestinal barrier. Treatment with sibofimloc did not reduce NEC incidence (100% in sibofimloc in formula controls) or severity, whereas DHM-fed piglets experienced 0% NEC. Sibofimloc-treated animals exhibited significantly reduced crypt depths, demonstrating heightened mucosal injury and impaired regenerative capacity. WGS revealed that sibofimloc-treated animals maintained a gut luminal microbiota composition similar to untreated formula controls, dominated by Clostridium perfringens (C. perfringens). Selective targeting of FimH-expressing Enterobacteriaceae was insufficient to prevent NEC or alter the gut microbiota in this preterm piglet model, underscoring the complexity of NEC-associated microbial communities and suggesting that additional microbial targets and other colonization mechanisms may contribute to disease development.

title: HSF1 inhibition potentiates the antifungal activity and proteome instability induced by the fungal Hsp110 inhibitor 2H
content: Fungal infections remain a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide; however, therapeutic options are limited and are increasingly compromised by antifungal resistance. Heat Shock Protein 110 kDa (Hsp110) is an essential molecular chaperone required for protein homeostasis (proteostasis) and fungal viability and has recently emerged as a promising antifungal target. We previously identified 2H, a first-in-class inhibitor of fungal Hsp110 proteins that exhibits broad-spectrum antifungal activity through disruption of proteostasis. Heat Shock Transcription Factor 1 (HSF1), the master regulator of cellular stress responses and chaperone expression, has also been proposed as a potential antifungal target, although direct pharmacological evidence supporting this strategy remains limited. Here, we investigated the effects of combining the HSF1 inhibitor DTHIB with the fungal Hsp110 inhibitor 2H in Cryptococcus neoformans and Candida albicans. Although DTHIB alone exhibited minimal antifungal activity, it significantly enhanced the growth-inhibitory and fungicidal effects of 2H. Notably, this potentiating effect was specific to 2H and was not observed with fluconazole. Consistent with the roles of Hsp110 and HSF1 in proteostasis, 2H induced extensive accumulation of detergent-insoluble protein aggregates in C. neoformans, whereas HSF1 inhibition further increased both the abundance and diversity of aggregated proteins. Quantitative proteomic analyses demonstrated that 2H induces proteome-wide protein aggregation, impacting proteins involved in a broad range of essential cellular processes, with high-molecular-weight proteins exhibiting particular susceptibility. Together, these findings provide pharmacological evidence supporting HSF1 as a promising antifungal sensitization target and demonstrate the utility of 2H as a chemical probe for studying Hsp110-dependent proteostasis. Simultaneous disruption of both HSF1-mediated stress responses and Hsp110-dependent proteostasis promotes extensive proteome instability and enhances antifungal activity, highlighting a potential new strategy for antifungal drug development.

title: HIV-1 envelope glycan loss links receptor adaptation and innate immune escape in SHIVs
content: Simian-human immunodeficiency viruses (SHIVs) are widely used to model HIV-1 infection in macaques, yet most SHIVs encoding circulating HIV-1 envelope glycoproteins (Env) replicate poorly because of inefficient use of macaque CD4 and sensitivity to host antiviral responses. During adaptation to macaques, Env is therefore subject to multiple selective pressures to improve receptor utilization while maintaining function in the face of host immune restriction. Type I interferon (IFN) is a major component of the host antiviral response during acute infection, and IFN resistance increases during SHIV adaptation to macaques through serial passage. However, the viral determinants of this resistance have remained unclear. Here, we show that serial passage of a lineage of SHIVs in macaques selected Env variants with markedly increased resistance to IFN- and enhanced replication in macaque CD4+ T lymphocytes. IFN- resistance mapped principally to loss of two highly conserved N-linked glycans at N197 and N276 near the CD4-binding site. Glycan loss altered the conformational landscape of virus-associated Env, enhanced macaque CD4-dependent entry and membrane fusion without increasing human CD4-dependent entry, and reduced incorporation of the IFN-inducible restriction factors IFITM3 and IFITM3A into progeny virions. Depletion of IFITM3/3A rendered the parental SHIV highly resistant to IFN- and abolished differential IFN- sensitivity among parental, adapted, and glycan-loss viruses. These findings reveal that loss of receptor-proximal Env glycans can simultaneously improve utilization of a heterologous CD4 receptor and promote escape from IFN-mediated restriction, linking receptor adaptation and innate immune evasion during lentiviral adaptation to a new host.

title: The mitochondrial transaminase GOT2 supports Japanese encephalitis virus replication in neuronal cells
content: Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is the leading cause of viral encephalitis in Asia, yet the host pathways that sustain its replication in the central nervous system remain poorly defined, and no antiviral therapies exist. Here we combine time-resolved transcriptomics and proteomics in mouse neuroblastoma (Neuro-2a) cells with time-resolved proteomics of infected mouse brain, integrated using directionality-penalized p-value merging. JEV infection was accompanied by progressive induction of interferon-stimulated proteins and by changes in the abundance of enzymes of central carbon and energy metabolism, spanning the tricarboxylic acid cycle, glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation and glutaminolysis. Temporal clustering of the brain proteome linked oxidative phosphorylation remodelling to a dependence on glutamine metabolism. Glutamine antagonism with DON reduced viral RNA, whereas glycolytic inhibition and AKT modulation did not significantly alter it under the conditions tested. Silencing of the mitochondrial transaminase GOT2 reduced JEV RNA, viral protein, and infectious virus production in human SH-SY5Y cells. Our findings identify a glutamine-GOT2 axis as a metabolic dependency of JEV and a candidate host-directed antiviral target.

title: Sex in the City: Reproductive Behaviors of Dragonflies across an Urban Landscape
content: Anthropogenic cityscapes provide complex habitats that influence animal communication and movement patterns, which are generally understudied in aquatic and semi-aquatic organisms. Community science, referring to public participation in scientific research, is an important tool for recording occurrence records and behavioral observations of understudied urban species. Boise, Idaho (USA), one of the fastest-growing cities in North America, has a long-established community science program for documenting occurrences of the semi-aquatic insect order Odonata (dragonflies and damselflies), making the city an ideal study system for comparing behavioral observations from community science with observations recorded using AI driven iNaturalist. In this study, we test the accuracy of iNaturalist observations and volunteer surveys to characterize dragonfly reproductive behaviors (tandem flight and tandem perching, oviposition, and mating) in the city, and use these observations to determine which dragonflies are using the urban landscape as reproductive habitat. The total numbers of species observations by volunteers and on iNaturalist in Boise were strongly correlated, while reproductive observations showed a strong observational threshold, as reproductive behaviors were rarely identified in less-observed species. iNaturalist tended to underrepresent total occurrences of ''flyer'' species, which rarely perch, while volunteer surveys underrepresented occurrences and reproductive behaviors of a more cyclical species that did not appear to be abundant in the field season in which this study was conducted. Our findings suggest that Boise provides suitable breeding habitat for both migratory and resident dragonflies. Species distribution models of three migratory and three putatively migratory species further demonstrate that these species would be expected in southwestern Idaho regardless of the presence of a city, and have persisted through urban development. This research demonstrates the value of community science in conducting basic research on understudied urban-dwelling species, although findings must be considered alongside potential biases.

title: From individuals to ecosystems: carrion beetle responses to heatwaves impact nutrient cycling
content: Climate extremes, such as heatwaves, are becoming more frequent and severe, leading to significant disruptions in key ecosystem processes. The direct effects of heatwaves on these processes have thus received increasing attention, yet the indirect effects of heatwaves, as mediated through animal behavioural responses, are still unknown. Insects play a fundamental role in carrion decomposition by modifying carcasses and regulating nutrient transfer to soils. Understanding how insect responses to climate extremes scale up to ecosystem processes is therefore crucial. In this study, we used a widespread carrion beetle, the burying beetle Nicrophorus vespilloides, to experimentally investigate the direct and indirect effects of a simulated heatwave on carrion decomposition dynamics, and the consequences for soil nutrient cycling. We found that burying beetle presence increased carcass mass loss by 355% under ambient temperatures, and that this was accompanied by significant increases in dissolved organic carbon (+86%), ammonium (+71%), and nitrate (+47%) concentrations. However, the positive effects of burying beetle presence on carcass mass loss were severely diminished by heat stress. Path analyses revealed that this was related to marked reductions in certain beetle behaviours, such as carcass preparation, as well as a reduction in brood size. These behavioural and reproductive shifts were, in turn, linked to decreased soil nitrate concentrations and soil moisture. Together, these findings demonstrate that the indirect effects of heatwaves on decomposition processes, as mediated by shifts in the behaviour and traits of animal ecosystem engineers, can be as important as their direct effects. Such indirect effects must therefore be incorporated into our understanding of how key ecosystem processes respond to climate extremes.

title: Climate change effects on terpene expression differ among populations and have consequences for herbivory in an invasive plant
content: ABSTRACT 1. Plant secondary metabolites often moderate interactions with abiotic and biotic factors. For example, secondary metabolites often deter insect herbivores from and influence the extent of damage to plant tissues. However, little is known about how climate change may alter the expression of secondary metabolites and the nature of the resulting effects on plant-herbivore interactions. As climate change continues to shift environmental conditions away from historical norms, climate change effects on plant-herbivore interactions may have important consequences for the range expansion of invasive plants and the efficacy of biocontrol agents across the range. 2. In this study, we examined climate change effects on terpene expression in common tansy (Tanacetum vulgare) in four field transplant sites in Minnesota, U.S.A. that include experimental manipulation of precipitation and temperature. Each transplant site included genotypes from 10 natural populations that span climate variation across Minnesota. We quantified leaf terpene profiles in two years (2024 and 2025) using targeted gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. We surveyed insect herbivory to the same genotypes in experimental field sites to ask how terpene profiles and chemotypes contribute to the likelihood of herbivory. 3. We detected evidence that climate change manipulation altered terpene production and depended on source population. Similarly, the extent of temporal variation in terpene profiles depended upon source population. We also found variation in terpene profiles among sites, further emphasizing the role of the environment in shaping terpene production. These shifts in terpene profiles, in turn, influenced the likelihood of herbivory. Herbivory was higher at the southern compared to northern sites and susceptibility to herbivory was higher in the northern compared to southern populations, particularly at northern sites where average herbivory was lower. The likelihood of herbivory also varied among chemotypes and the frequency of chemotypes varied among source populations, suggesting a complex interplay between the historical and current environments, terpene production, and plant-herbivore interactions. 4. Synthesis. Together, our results suggest a combined role of the abiotic environment and population differentiation in moderating plant-herbivore interactions via shifts and variation in terpene profiles, which may influence invasive range dynamics and complicate the regional management strategies of common tansy.

title: The dynamic face of rarity: tracking species at risk beyond space
content: Avoid extinction of rare species is critical for biodiversity conservation. Rabinowitz proposes rare species is pattern that emerge from combination of three parameters: geographical range, habitat specificity and population size. Several papers have been looked to improves this method over last years, but they often neglect the temporal dimension, crucial for understanding the extinction process. This study introduces a dynamic framework that model the three dimensions of rarity as a continuous three-dimensional space, integrating vector-based representations and an ecological vector field to quantify rarity, temporal dynamics, displacement and equilibrium. Derivative equations are used to describe the temporal evolution in that system which is integrate to account the shift in that space. This framework allows to reinterpret ecological change as a trajectory though space, where each axis corresponds to an ecological dimension. This multidimensional representation distinguishes intrinsic rarity from extinction risk and can identify demographic declines, habitat restriction, or range contraction. The method can be applied to a single species or a set of species, using short or long sampling time intervals. A test across freshwater fish, birds, amphibians, and terrestrial plants showed that rarity dimensions can change independently among species. By monitoring the shifts in this dimension simultaneity, we can plan the conservation by priority species that are shaking their dimensions over time. Unlike static assessments that already exist, this method provides a nuanced understanding of a rare species vulnerability as a dynamic representation of temporal changes. An R package and application guide are provided, helping conservation practitioners use this approach.

title: How does the community structure of dung beetles affect ecosystem functions? Modeling of secondary seed dispersal and seedling establishment.
content: Dung beetles are associated with diverse ecosystem functions. However, their populations are declining globally, raising concerns about the loss of ecosystem functions. Among these services, secondary seed dispersal is crucial for plant recruitment and movement. To reveal the relationship between community composition and ecosystem function, I developed a novel mathematical model simulating seedling establishment that accounts for seed dispersal by two functional groups (tunnelers and rollers), seed predation, and among-seedling competition. The model revealed that when seed predators were absent, rollers contributed more to seedling establishment than tunnelers; consequently, communities with a high proportion of rollers and a low proportion of tunnelers maximized the number of established seedlings. Under high predation pressure, tunneler-abundant communities yielded greater seedling establishment. Under intermediate predation pressure, the relative contributions of the two functional groups depended on the intensity of among-seedling competition: tunnelers enhanced establishment when competition was weak, whereas rollers excelled when competition was strong. This study provides the first mathematical framework for dung beetle-mediated secondary seed dispersal, advancing our understanding of the links between community composition and ecosystem functioning. These findings offer critical insights for anthropogenic biodiversity management, such as the conservation and introduction of dung beetle communities.

title: Hidden grassland productivity from overlooked herbivore impacts
content: Grasslands cover approximately 40% of Earth's land surface and contribute substantially to terrestrial primary production. Despite widespread grazing, field estimates of grassland aboveground net primary productivity commonly overlook two grazing-related processes: biomass consumed by herbivores and post-grazing compensatory growth. The magnitude and direction of the resulting biases remain unclear. Here we quantified these biases using a 3-year yak grazing experiment on the Tibetan Plateau, a meta-analysis of 152 grazing experiments across China, and a global synthesis of 212 paired observations from 58 studies. Overlooking biomass consumed by herbivores consistently underestimated productivity by 34-51%. By contrast, overlooking grazing-induced compensation generated smaller but more variable biases, ranging from 29% underestimation to 19% overestimation, mainly reflecting contrasting compensatory responses under rotational versus continuous grazing. These findings show that overlooking grazing-mediated processes introduces substantial, process-dependent biases in grassland productivity estimates, underscoring the need to incorporate these processes into ecosystem and climate assessments.

title: Mercury bioaccumulation varies across breeding-site height and life-history traits in Amazonian phytotelm-breeding frogs
content: Mercury (Hg) concentrations in the environment have significantly increased in the Amazon. Despite the observed deleterious effects on freshwater wildlife, the impacts of Hg contamination in phytotelmata (i.e., waterbodies contained in plant structures) and the species therein remain undocumented. We investigated the effects of Hg contamination on a phytotelm-breeding frog community in an otherwise pristine rainforest in French Guiana. Total Hg concentrations were measured in 28 pools at different heights (i.e. ground to canopy), and in the bodies of 103 tadpoles from five species with contrasting life histories. Tadpoles from ground pools had higher Hg concentrations than those from arboreal pools, revealing a vertical gradient in Hg contamination; tadpoles from species with slow development and parental care (i.e., tadpole transport) exhibited higher Hg concentrations than those of species with fast development without parental care. Finally, although Hg burdens were not associated with oxidative DNA levels, individuals reaching metamorphosis exhibited lower DNA damage than early-stage tadpoles, possibly reflecting reduced oxidative damage resulting from cellular remodelling undergone during metamorphosis, or selective mortality processes. Our findings highlight the joint influence of habitat type and life-history traits on Hg accumulation and that, even in pristine forests, Hg exposure varies strongly across microhabitats and species.

title: Avian uropygial secretions as a novel bioinsecticide for mosquito vector control
content: Background: Malaria control relies heavily on interventions targeting mosquito vectors, but the rapid emergence of insecticide resistance threatens the effectiveness of existing approaches. Identifying novel, effective, and environmentally sustainable insecticides is therefore a priority. Birds produce uropygial secretions with well-documented antimicrobial properties, but their potential insecticidal activity against mosquitoes, including malaria vectors, remains unexplored. Methods: We evaluated the insecticidal activity of uropygial secretions from wild house sparrows (Passer domesticus) against the malaria vector Anopheles stephensi and four additional mosquito species of medical importance (Aedes aegypti, Aedes albopictus, Culex pipiens, and Culiseta longiareolata). A total of 2,293 adult mosquitoes were tested using CDC bottle bioassays at three secretion concentrations (0.5, 0.25, and 0.125) and an untreated control. Mosquito mortality was monitored for 120 min. Results: Uropygial secretions caused substantial mosquito knockdown/mortality, with effects increasing with concentration and exposure time. Susceptibility differed significantly among species after 120 min. Notably, An. stephensi was particularly susceptible, reaching knockdown/mortality of 92%, 94%, and 83% at 0.5, 0.25, and 0.125 concentrations, respectively. Conclusions: Our findings provide the first experimental evidence that avian uropygial secretions possess direct insecticidal activity against mosquitoes and identify them as a previously overlooked source of naturally derived insecticidal compounds. The high susceptibility of An. stephensi highlights their potential relevance for developing novel bioinsecticides for malaria vector control.

title: Global failure to track international biodiversity targets on islands
content: Islands harbour exceptional biodiversity but face severe threats, making their conservation crucial to achieving the goals and targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. We therefore evaluated whether existing indicators can track progress toward the Framework's 23 targets across islands worldwide. We screened 504 biodiversity and socioeconomic indicators from the official framework and other global initiatives, retaining 47 indicators. Historical time series from 1950 onward were modelled and projected to 2030. Indicators were also classified using the Driver-Pressure-State-Impact-Response (DPSIR) and Theory of Change (ToC). Results showed uneven progress: eight targets improved across all available indicators, while ten displayed conflicting trends. Nearly half of the indicators focused on policy and management responses showed improvement, whereas trends in biodiversity pressures and states were mixed. Critically, 15 of 23 targets (65%) lacked a suitable headline indicator, and five targets had no indicator at all. Notably, Targets 2 and 8, addressing ecosystem restoration and climate change impacts, respectively, lacked island indicators entirely. Over half of the available indicators (29 of 47; 62%) were reported at the national level, limiting their applicability to subnational island jurisdictions and potentially obscuring differences between mainland and island conditions. Most targets also lacked quantitative objectives, limiting evaluation of whether the rate of change is sufficient to meet the targets by 2030. We recommend island-level reporting, island-specific indicators, and quantitative benchmarks tailored to island needs.

title: Intra- and interspecific relationships of alpine ungulates reorganise along a wolf recolonisation gradient
content: Apex predators are recovering across many ecosystems after decades of decline, yet whether their return can restore ecological interactions disrupted by their loss remains poorly understood. Here, we used the ongoing recolonisation of grey wolves (Canis lupus) in the south-eastern Alps as a natural gradient of predator recovery to examine how predation risk and human disturbance shape relationships among red deer (Cervus elaphus), roe deer (Capreolus capreolus), and Alpine chamois (Rupicapra rupicapra). Across a gradient of time since wolf establishment, roe deer increasingly occupied sites without red deer, suggesting predator recovery alters relationships between prey species. Red deer also formed larger groups, consistent with a shift in collective behaviour under increased predation risk. Human disturbance also affected group formation in red deer and chamois. Together, these findings show that prey community structure can vary with wolf recovery, even in human-dominated landscapes, through altered associations among species and grouping within species.

title: The conservation effectiveness of Indigenous and local community governance
content: Effective governance of natural areas is central to conserving biodiversity and Earth's life support systems, including climate regulation and food and water provisioning. Understanding the relative effectiveness of different governance options is thus critical. We conducted a global meta-analysis of 409 cases in 42 countries, comparing ecological outcomes over time in areas governed by Indigenous Peoples and local communities versus conventional governance approaches. Outcomes in community-governed areas matched those in conventional fully protected areas and exceeded those in partially protected and unprotected areas. Communities with legal land title had better outcomes than communities without title. We provide the strongest evidence to date that ecological outcomes of Indigenous and community governance meet or exceed those of other area-based conservation approaches and that titling strengthens these outcomes.

title: Beyond the urban surface: bird-borne sensing reveals the atmospheric structure of urban heat
content: Urban heat is commonly characterized near ground level, while its vertical atmospheric structure remains difficult to observe across cities. We used bird-borne temperature sensors on homing pigeons (Columba livia) and yellow-legged gulls (Larus michahellis) to investigate the horizontal, vertical and daytime structure of the lower urban atmosphere over Rome. The dataset comprised 61,917 air-temperature observations from 47 individuals of gulls and pigeons, spanning 17 km and altitudes up to 400 m above ground level. Generalized additive models related air temperature to distance from the city centre, altitude, time of day, land cover, tree-patch area and topography, and reconstructed three-dimensional temperature fields. Air temperature showed a centre-to-periphery gradient that weakened with altitude and through the daytime period. At 20 m above ground level, its magnitude declined from -0.40 {degrees}C km--1 at 09:00 to -0.30 {degrees}C km--1 at 13:00 and -0.19 {degrees}C km--1 at 17:00, with weaker gradients at higher altitudes. Reconstructed isothermal boundaries showed a complementary vertical pattern. At 13:00, median heights decreased from 135 m for the 34 {degrees}C boundary to 76 m for 35 {degrees}C and 37 m for 36 {degrees}C. The 34 {degrees}C boundary reached its greatest extent around midday, rising from 57 m at 09:00 to 135 m at 13:00 before declining to 14 m at 17:00. Horizontal thermal contrast and the vertical development of high-temperature air represent complementary dimensions of urban heat. Bird-borne sensing offers a promising approach for resolving three-dimensional atmospheric temperature patterns that conventional monitoring networks cannot capture.

title: DroneMegaDetector, A Generalised Model For Detecting Large Mammals In Aerial Imagery
content: Large-scale drone surveys can generate imagery across substantial geographic areas, but automated analysis remains challenging because animal appearance, target density, imaging conditions and target scale can vary considerably between surveys. We present a general-purpose RF-DETR Medium object detector developed for large-scale aerial drone imagery and evaluate its ability to generalise across taxa, environments and survey conditions. Unlike specialist counting systems that primarily return point detections, the proposed detector produces explicit bounding boxes, providing a spatial representation that can support counting as well as downstream detection, classification and tracking workflows. We evaluated the detector on an internal held-out test set and independent external datasets spanning cattle, birds, caribou and hippopotamuses, together with imagery acquired under substantially different survey conditions. On the comparative Cattle dataset, RF-DETR matched OWL across the reported point-localisation and counting metrics, while on Caribou it achieved almost identical point-based detection performance and similar aggregate counting error. Performance varied across the broader external benchmark, with reduced transfer to unseen avian imagery and differences between models across datasets. At high altitude on SAVMAP, all evaluated approaches experienced substantial performance degradation, demonstrating a shared limitation associated with small target scale. Overall, the results show that a general-purpose detector trained on heterogeneous drone imagery can provide competitive localisation and counting performance across diverse datasets while retaining explicit bounding-box outputs. The trained model weights and inference code are provided online to support reproducible large-scale aerial wildlife monitoring and further development of drone-based computer-vision workflows.
